sections.html:
East Fishkill sellers can list with an agent, sell on their own, or take a cash offer for the house as it stands. Cash fits best when the house needs work, a septic or certificate question is open, or you want a firm closing date. The offer will sit below a polished listing, so compare it with your payoff and closing costs.

Three local items tend to come up in any sale: the septic inspection rule, flood questions and the Building Department's permit records. Each is easier to settle before a buyer asks.

East Fishkill sits on the southern edge of Dutchess County and covers 56.53 square miles. Hamlets include Arthursburg, Fishkill Plains, Gayhead, Hopewell Junction, Peckslip and Stormville. Interstate 84 and the Taconic State Parkway both cross the town. Population is 29,801.

  • Owner-occupied homes: 90.6 percent
  • Middle-of-the-range home value (2020 to 2024): $478,400
  • Middle-of-the-range household income: $138,543
  • People per household: 2.92
  • Residents in the same house a year earlier: 95.3 percent
  • Average commute to work: 36.2 minutes

Most owners stay put, so gather the latest closed sales near your own street, not just a town figure. Describe highway access plainly in a listing, since the average commute is long.

Four districts reach into town: Arlington, Carmel, Pawling and Wappingers Central School Districts. The town's Receiver of Taxes collects school taxes for two of them, Wappingers and Carmel.

The district decides the school tax bill and its payment calendar, so read the property's current bill before you describe the house to a buyer. The next section shows how the dates differ.

County and town taxes are payable once a year, in January and February without penalty. The Receiver of Taxes works from 2464 Route 52 in Hopewell Junction, next to the police station, and also collects fire, lighting and park district charges.

East Fishkill county and town tax penalties
Payment windowPenalty
January 1 to February 28None
March2 percent
April3 percent
May4 percent plus $2

The books close on May 31, and unpaid balances move to the Dutchess County Commissioner of Finance about June 15.

School bills run on a different clock. Wappingers taxes are payable from mid-September into October, with a 2 percent penalty through the end of that month. Carmel taxes are payable in September, and that district alone allows a half payment with a 5 percent charge on each half. Unpaid school taxes are added to the next county and town bill.

The assessor values each parcel so school, county, town and special district taxes can be divided fairly, but the assessor does not set the tax rate. The calendar is short: taxable status date on March 1, tentative roll by May 1, Grievance Day on the 4th Tuesday of May, and the final roll on July 1, which is the roll that next year's taxes are based on.

Exemptions for seniors, firefighters and people with disabilities must be filed by March 1. STAR is filed directly with New York State, and the town asks residents not to call its office about it. Only the current tentative roll can be grieved, so a seller who thinks the value is wrong should raise it before the May hearing.

Three local rules can surface during a sale, and each is easier to handle before a buyer asks.

  • Septic: owners inside the East of Hudson Watershed must have each system pumped, cleaned and visually inspected by a registered water transporter at least every five years, and file the inspection form with the Building Department.
  • Flood: East Fishkill joined FEMA's Community Rating System in October 2015 as a Class 8 community, giving a 10 percent premium discount inside the Special Flood Hazard Area and 5 percent outside it. Homeowner policies do not pay flood losses, and a new flood policy has a five-day waiting period.
  • Water and sewer: the town runs 17 water districts and 6 sewer districts, billed every three months, with a 10 percent late fee after the first month and unpaid rents re-levied on the next tax bill after November 1.

Dutchess County's Parcel Access map can show whether a property lies in a flood area, and the Building Department can supply flood data to sellers and lenders.

The Building Department's process starts with a complete general permit application, then a pre-site inspection, plan review, permit issuance, inspections called in by the contractor, and a final certificate once the last inspection passes. A certificate of occupancy fee applies where relevant, and the town offers an online permit portal.

If you added a deck, finished a basement or built a garage, find the final certificate before you list. The Building Department sits on the lower level of Town Hall, with the entrance at the rear, and also houses the zoning officer and floodplain administrator.

Recording a deed with the Dutchess County Clerk costs $45, plus $5 per page, $5 for the capital gains affidavit that accompanies form TP-584, and a $10 residential deed notification fee. State transfer tax of two dollars per $500 of price is separate and goes in with the return within 15 days of delivery.

Your closing attorney can total these and confirm what applies to your deed.

Pull together your latest county and town and school bills, the septic inspection form if you are in the watershed, any flood policy, and the permit certificates for work done. Then ask for offers and compare each with what you owe. A cash buyer will usually take the house as it stands, which spares you repairs and showings.

Closing day brings payoffs from your proceeds, delivery of the deed, and the transfer tax return within 15 days. Ask the Receiver of Taxes for a payoff on any open bill, since balances left after May 31 move to the Dutchess County Commissioner of Finance.

If the house is inside the East of Hudson Watershed, have the septic pumped and inspected before you list and file the form with the Building Department, so a buyer sees a finished record. If you are not sure whether a flood policy is needed, check the county's Parcel Access map and keep the result with your sale papers. Water and sewer rents are billed every three months, so ask the town for a current balance before closing.

faqs.q: Is East Fishkill in Dutchess County?
faqs.a: Yes. East Fishkill sits on the southern border of Dutchess County and became its own town on November 29, 1849. Its tax office is on Route 52 in Hopewell Junction.

faqs.q: What do East Fishkill homes typically sell for?
faqs.a: The middle value for owner-occupied homes is $478,400 for 2020 to 2024. That is a survey figure, so recent sales on your own street are the better guide to a price.

faqs.q: When is the last day to pay county and town taxes without a penalty?
faqs.a: February 28. A 2 percent charge applies in March, 3 percent in April, and 4 percent plus $2 in May, after which the county takes over collection.

faqs.q: Do East Fishkill septic systems need inspections before a sale?
faqs.a: Systems inside the East of Hudson Watershed must be pumped and inspected at least once every five years under the Town Code. Ask the Building Department whether your property lies in the watershed area.

faqs.q: Who sets property assessments in East Fishkill?
faqs.a: The Town Assessor values each property, and Grievance Day is the 4th Tuesday in May. The assessor cannot change the tax rate, which comes from the school, county, town and district budgets.
